title: The Rivets on Jacob Davis's Table and the Letter to Levi Strauss
dek: A Reno tailor who could not afford another patent fee offered his cloth supplier half the rights to riveted work trousers, and the patent was granted in 1873.

story.event: A Reno tailor's riveted work trousers and the shared patent of 1873
story.summary: In January 1871 Jacob Davis, a tailor in Reno, Nevada, riveted the pockets of a pair of work trousers using rivets he used on horse blankets, and went on to make about 200 pairs. Unable to risk another patent fee, he wrote to his cloth supplier Levi Strauss offering half the rights if Strauss backed the patent; the application was filed in August 1872 and patent 139,121 was granted to Davis and Levi Strauss & Company on 20 May 1873. Davis moved to San Francisco to run production and stayed until his death in 1908.
paragraphs: In the first week of January 1871, in Reno, Nevada, the tailor Jacob Davis made a pair of cheap work trousers from white cotton duck. A woman from across the railway track had ordered them for her husband, a large, poor labouring man who was ill and could find nothing in the shops to fit. She measured him with a knotted string, paid three dollars in advance and asked for the trousers to be strong, because he tore his clothes. Davis was also making horse blankets for teamsters, their straps fastened with rivets. When the trousers were done, he said under oath in 1874, "the rivets were lying on the table and the thought struck me" to fasten the pockets with them.

He made little of it at first. By his account he made about ten pairs that February and perhaps a dozen in March, mostly for teamsters and surveyors, and roughly 200 before he applied for a patent. Other tailors began copying the idea. Davis wanted protection and knew the cost. According to the genealogist Kathleen Paini Clemence, each of his patent applications had cost $68, and his wife Annie, then caring for five children under seven, would not see another $68 risked.

He turned to his San Francisco cloth supplier, Levi Strauss, who Davis testified was the first person he told about the rivets. In his letter, as quoted from a family transcript, he offered Strauss "half the right to sell all such Clothing Revited according to the Patent, for all the Pacific States and Teroterous" in return for paying for the patent. Strauss agreed. The application was filed on 9 August 1872 in Davis's name, assigned to himself and Levi Strauss & Company, and was reworked more than once before patent 139,121 was granted on 20 May 1873.

By the end of April 1873 Davis had moved to San Francisco to run production for Strauss, at first with seamstresses working from home and later in a factory. Within a year the partners were in court defending the patent; in February 1875 they won, though with $2,000 in damages rather than the $20,000 they had claimed. Davis ran the factory until his death in 1908, and his son Simon took over after him.

quote.text: What work soever any mortal doth Of body, mind, or speech, evil or good, By these five doth he that. Which being thus, Whoso, for lack of knowledge, seeth himself As the sole actor, knoweth nought at all And seeth nought.
quote.locator: Chapter XVIII, "Religion by Deliverance and Renunciation" (verses 15-16 in the usual numbering)
quote.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gîtâ, tr. Sir Edwin Arnold, Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
quote.connection: Davis swore that he was the inventor, and he was. But the trousers had other makers too: a woman's request, a knotted string, rivets left over from horse blankets, Strauss's cloth and Strauss's money. Offering half the rights was, among other things, an admission of that.

reflection: Davis had the idea, the customers and two hundred pairs of proof. What he did not have was $68 he could afford to lose, and at home there was a clear limit on how many more times he could try alone. Whatever he felt about that, he wrote a letter and offered half.

You may be carrying something that could go further with another person's money, skill or reach, and sharing it can feel like giving away what is yours. Davis kept the work he was good at for the rest of his life. A fair share offered early is sometimes what lets a thing exist at all.
invitation: Name one thing you are trying to do alone that someone else could help carry. Write down what you would be willing to offer them in return, and leave the decision itself for another day.

research_notes: Dates of the first riveted pair: Davis's sworn deposition of 17 June 1874 says the first week of January 1871 (the woman wanted them before New Year but he finished them after), which DocsTeach and the National Archives blog follow; Kate Kelly (America Comes Alive) says 1870 and Wikipedia says December 1870, which fits the order rather than the making. The story uses January 1871. The customer: the deposition calls him a large, poor labouring man, sick (the transcriber marks the illness, 'dropsy', as uncertain), whose wife wanted to send him to chop wood; the story does not name the illness. Who thought of the rivets: Davis testified that he noticed them on his table himself; the Jewish Museum of the American West says a customer suggested it. The story follows the deposition. Number of pairs: the deposition gives about 200 before the patent application, as do Kelly and Harrison. The $68 fee and Annie's refusal to risk it come only from the genealogist Kathleen Paini Clemence, interviewed by San Diego Jewish World, and are attributed to her; HISTORY.com says only that Davis lacked the money for the paperwork. The letter wording ('Revited', 'Teroterous') is Davis's spelling as quoted by Kelly from the Ben Davis Company's transcript, which is no longer online; the original letter was not seen. Kelly says an earlier application was turned down before Davis wrote to Strauss; JMAW says the joint application was first turned down as too broad; Clemence says it was reworked several times; the story says only that it was reworked more than once. Davis's move date comes from his deposition ('April 26 a year ago', i.e. 1873). Davis's birth year differs (1831 in Kelly and Harrison, 1834 in JMAW) and is not used. Founder field names both men because the patent and the company are shared; the episode is told mainly from Davis's side. The Levi Strauss & Co. company pages (levistrauss.com) load but give only an outline. The Gita passage is Krishna's teaching on the five factors of every act (verses 14-16 in the usual numbering); the excerpt corresponds to verses 15-16.
